title: Call Centres Shrink by Not Hiring: AI's First Labour-Market Canary
summary: Global call-centre headcount is falling for the first time in a decade, and it is happening through fewer new hires rather than layoffs. We connect Revelio's data, the customer-support productivity study, the 19% gap for young workers and the Danish nulls into one consistent story, and look at what the EU chatbot rules mean for building automation in the Netherlands.
shownotes:
The signal: Revelio Labs finds global call-centre headcount 5.3% below its December 2023 peak, shrinking through lower entry rates rather than layoffs.
The micro mechanism: Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond show a GPT-based assistant raises support productivity 15%, mostly for novices, flattening the experience curve.
From productivity to headcount: why inelastic demand plus high turnover predicts fewer hires, not layoffs.
The US payroll evidence: the August 2026 Canaries update finds workers aged 22-25 in AI-exposed occupations 19% below their less-exposed peers, and its caveats.
The counter-evidence: Danish nulls on earnings and hours, the CFO survey, and the Chicago CPS study, and why they measure incumbents rather than inflows.
Where displaced workers go, and the EU/Dutch constraints: AI Act Article 50 disclosure and the right to human intervention for distance financial services.
Takeaways: a Dutch entry-rate replication with CBS data (SBI 82.20), a chatbot compliance audit for SMEs, and keeping experts in the loop of your own AI tools.
